This sequence mirrors the human process: becoming aware of a gap in understanding, seeking external input, and returning with new clarity. It reinforces the idea that both biological and artificial systems thrive best when they have a functional mechanism for assessing their knowledge, recognizing when they don’t know, and knowing how to respond next. We will discuss the biological version of AI hallucinations, the breakdown of this metacognitive step, a bit later when we discuss the Dunning–Kruger effect. Just as a human learner becomes more attentive when uncertain or when they discover that they were confident and wrong, AI systems are being taught to pause when “confidence” is low. But the parallel goes further. Rather than simply accepting the gap, the model is trained to seek: to initiate a real-time search—often across the web—for new information that might clarify or resolve the uncertainty. Once that additional context is retrieved, it is integrated into the model’s working memory and used to generate a more informed response. In essence, the AI learns to recognize its limitations, activate external inquiry, and then revisit the task with an expanded awareness. This process—pause, search, integrate, respond—is not unlike the recursive way humans deepen understanding through curiosity, exploration, and reflection. As with human cognition, intelligence here is not defined by always knowing the answer but by knowing how to respond when you don’t. As we continue, we’ll explore how these memory systems—both human and artificial—are not just about storage. They are about construction. They are active, dynamic— predictive . And in both systems, memory is not passive—it is a central element of intelligence . The Emergence of Something Different Biological brains, forged by evolution and refined by necessity, have been our only known locus of thought, imagination, and creativity. Intelligence, as we understood it, was biological and embodied by definition. It breathed, it blinked, it aged. And then, suddenly, it didn’t. When DeepMind’s AlphaGo AI defeated world champion Lee Sedol in 2016, something fundamental shifted. 35 This wasn’t mimicry. This was originality. It wasn’t just fast computing. It was simulating something that felt like intuition—born not of consciousness but of pattern. But we must be careful here. AlphaGo didn’t feel the joy of victory. It had no awareness. No curiosity. It was a savant without a soul. Still, it had proven something extraordinary: That intelligence is not exclusive to biological systems. And AlphaGo had no body. No life history. It was pure structure and energy. Intelligence had escaped biology. This was the first real sign that the emergence of high-level intelligence could exist outside a biological brain. And that’s the critical shift: • Human intelligence is constrained by fixed constraints of time, energy, biology, and other factors. • Artificial intelligence is constrained by architecture, training data, and compute. Chips get faster at an accelerating pace, throughput per chip is accelerating rapidly, and AI can be plugged into the power grid, increasing abundance rather than fixed constraint, while leveraging the findings of our biology hyperefficient intelligence evolution. Intelligence, once confined to biology and constraint, has found new fuel. Better at Sharing Hinton also famously states that AI is a better computational learning engine than humans because “they’re billions of times better than us at sharing information.” Let’s unpack that a bit. Imagine one million Tesla fully self-driving AI cars on the road. Each one engaged in the constraints of moving around in a messy and complex physical world. However, they are all connected to a central AI brain in addition to the AI in the individual car. Meaning, what one Tesla self-driving AI car learns, they all learn. As humans, we have not found a way to do that. If we are now no longer the only system in the universe capable of learning, the question then becomes: Are we the only ones capable of understanding? Understanding: The Compost and the Bomb “What do a compost heap and a nuclear bomb have in common?” It’s a question that, at first glance, seems absurd. One decomposes organic matter slowly; the other obliterates everything around it in an instant. When Geoffrey Hinton asked humans that question, the most common response was confusion or silence. But when Hinton asked this of an AI neural network—trained not only on language but on deep pattern association—it responded: “They are both uncontrolled chain reactions. That in both cases, an initiating event triggers a self-perpetuating cascade.” This was more than clever wordplay. It was an illustration of some form of pattern recognition that required a fairly high level of understanding to find. The model didn’t arrive at this insight by recalling a memorized phrase or through statistical next-word prediction alone. It synthesized an abstract connection by identifying a structural similarity. In both cases, a chain reaction is triggered where the output of one step becomes the fuel for the next. In a compost heap, microbial decomposition releases heat, which in turn accelerates further microbial activity, deepening the slow cycle of decay. In a nuclear bomb, the splitting of atomic nuclei releases neutrons, which then collide with other nuclei, causing them to split and release more energy in a runaway explosion. One is slow, organic, and life-giving. The other is instantaneous, engineered, and destructive. But both obey the same underlying principle: a chain reaction that compounds itself once set in motion. To Hinton, this response was profound. It suggested that the system had done more than mimic intelligence—it had exhibited a form of understanding . The AI was not simply regurgitating facts; it was drawing inferences across domains, compressing complexity into metaphor, and offering up a novel synthesis. In the context of our discussion, this matters deeply. It underscores a pivotal shift: The intelligence that we ignited in silicon is beginning to form its own models of the world.
